newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi Kurdish foes dig in as U.S. seeks ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi Kurdish foes dig in as U.S. seeks ceasefire.

text.p: Kurdish rebels massed forces near a city held by a rival Baghdad-backed faction, as the United States said it would start intensive efforts to broker a ceasefire in the inter-Kurdish conflict.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday officials from the warring factions would meet Assistant Secretary for Near Eastern Affairs Robert Pelletreau in Washington on Thursday.
He said Pelletreau would travel to the region at the weekend to meet the leaders of the two groups -- the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).

Burns said the aim of Pelletreau's separate talks with KDP leader Massoud Barzani and the PUK's Jalal Talabani was to "convince them that it is in their immediate interest to move towards a ceasefire and not to allow Iran or Iraq the opportunity to inflame the situation further".

Barzani's Baghdad-backed group has accused neighbouring Iran of sending men and munitions across the border to help Talabani, as a part of the regional rivalry between Tehran and Baghdad. Iran denies this.

Earlier on Wednesday the PUK said 6,000 of its fighters were gathering at Barisan Valley 70 km (44 miles) northeast of the city of Arbil but it was not immediately known if the PUK forces would attack the city, home for some 800,000 people.
The KDP captured the city six weeks ago with help from tank-led Iraqi troops, in an assault that enraged Washington.
The United States fired missiles at military targets in southern Iraq in response to the fall of Arbil, which ruined U.S. aid, military and intelligence efforts in north Iraq.
Talabani said after his fighters recaptured most of the ground they lost in September he would not storm Arbil.
The United States leads a Western allied air force that shields the Kurds from any attack by Iraqi forces.
President Saddam Hussein sent an envoy to Tehran on Tuesday with a message for Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Iran's official news agency IRNA said.

"The Iraqi envoy voiced Iraq's desire for good neighbourly relations with Iran and for expansion of mutual relations. He also called for cooperation and exchange of views between the two countries on regional issues," IRNA said. It did not name the envoy.
Meanwhile, Iran expressed regret over remarks by Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller that Tehran might be meddling in inter-Kurdish fighting in northern Iraq.
IRNA said an Iranian foreign ministry source regretted the remarks and reiterated Iran's denial that it backed the PUK in its drive against the Baghdad-backed KDP.
